international.title: Andy Burnham to give update to MPs after ‘landmark’ UK-EU summit – UK politics live
international.summary: PM expected to tell Commons that Friday’s deal will be ‘the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament’ Louise Haigh , the first secretary of state, has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos. In a story in the Times today, Patrick Maguire says: The Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs. Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the construction of infrastructure. We’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for. For far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure. That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale. This government will put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology. Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best. The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate. Challenging the misconception that public control means wholesale nationalisation, the first secretary will say this approach is not about whether or not markets work, but how effective monopolies have resulted in a lack of genuine competition.
